title: How an enum's constants and statics are built

questions.stem: Per this page, which access may an enum's constructor have?

options.text: Public, so that other classes can create more constants of the enum
options.says: The page says an enum constructor cannot be public; the constants are the enum's only instances.

options.text: Protected, so that constant bodies in subclasses can call the constructor
options.says: The page says an enum constructor cannot be protected either; constant bodies still run through the enum's own constructor.

options.text: Private only, which also holds when no access modifier is written at all
options.says: The page says enum constructors are implicitly private and cannot be public or protected.

questions.stem: An enum `Color` declares `private static final Map<String, Color> MAP`, and its constructor calls a static method that puts the new constant into `MAP`. Per this page, what happens when `Color` is initialized?

options.text: It throws NullPointerException, because MAP is still null while the constants are created
options.says: The page says static fields are initialized after all constants exist, so reaching MAP indirectly from the constructor finds it null and throws NullPointerException.

options.text: It fails to compile, because the compiler rejects every call from a constructor to a static method
options.says: The page says only a direct reference to the static field is a compile error; reaching it through a static method compiles and fails at run time.

options.text: It registers every constant, because MAP is initialized before the first constant is created
options.says: The page says the order is the other way round: the constants are created first and static fields such as MAP afterwards.

origin.section: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
